title: Universal property of componentwise normalization for a normal source
statement:
Let $X$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] such that every quasi-compact open has finitely many irreducible components [def-weil-irreducible-components], and let $g:Y	o X$ be a morphism from a scheme whose local rings are integrally closed domains [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Suppose that each irreducible component $C$ of $Y$ dominates an irreducible component $D$ of $X$, meaning that the closure of $g(C)$ in $X$ is $D$. For the componentwise normalization $
u_X:X^
u	o X$ [def-weil-pbc-reduced-normalization], there exists a unique morphism $h:Y	o X^
u$ such that $
u_X\circ h=g$. No integral-morphism, component-bijection, generic-field-isomorphism, quasi-compactness or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed on $g$ or $Y$. The empty source is allowed.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, part (4); Tag 0CDV, label lemma-normalization-in-terms-of-components, identifies the componentwise construction.

proof.text:
Every local ring of $Y$ is a domain, hence has no nonzero nilpotent element; thus $Y$ is reduced. The reduced-source factorization lemma gives $g=i_X\circ g_0$ with $g_0:Y	o X_{\mathrm{red}}$. Reduction leaves the underlying topological space unchanged, so quasi-compact opens and their irreducible components are unchanged; the finiteness hypothesis on the target therefore still holds. The same topological identification preserves the closure of each component image, so every component of $Y$ still dominates a component of $X_{\mathrm{red}}$ under $g_0$. The reduced induced scheme on each component is the same for $X$ and $X_{\mathrm{red}}$: on an affine chart its vanishing prime contains the nilradical, so quotienting first by the nilradical and then by that prime gives the same quotient ring. The definition of componentwise normalization therefore gives the same summands, maps, and coproduct for both schemes. It is enough to prove the result with $X$ reduced and $g=g_0$. A factorization through $X^
u$ for the original $g$ is also one over $X_{\mathrm{red}}$, since $i_X$ is a closed immersion and hence a monomorphism by the closed-immersion characterization (closed immersion if and only if proper and a monomorphism): from $i_X\circ(
u_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}\circ h)=g=i_X\circ g_0$ we get $
u_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}\circ h=g_0$, because $
u_X=i_X\circ
u_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}$ summand by summand.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, proof of (4), reduction to the reduced target; componentwise definition makes reduction compatibility immediate

proof.text: For an arbitrary pair of affine opens $W=\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq Y$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq X$ with $g(W)\subseteq U$, write $\varphi:A\to B$ for the restricted map. Such $W$ cover $Y$, by taking an affine neighbourhood of $g(y)$ and then an affine neighbourhood of $y$ in its inverse image. The affine stalk comparison identifies $B_{\mathfrak q}$ with $\mathcal O_{Y,\mathfrak q}$ for every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$; hence $B$ is a normal ring in the local-ring sense. Both $A$ and $B$ are reduced. The reduced target retains the hypothesis on quasi-compact opens by step 1, so the affine normalization-chart lemma applies; it imposes no condition on the components of $W$. Thus $\nu^{-1}(U)=\operatorname{Spec}\overline A$, where $\overline A$ is the integral closure of $A$ in $Q(A)$ and the structural map is $a\mapsto a/1$.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, proof of (4), affine W and U; Tag 035P via the cited chart node

proof.text: For a minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$, its closed subset $V(\mathfrak q)$ is an irreducible component of $W$. Take an irreducible component $C$ of $Y$ containing its closure in $Y$. Since $C$ meets $W$, $C\cap W$ is an irreducible component of $W$; maximality forces $C\cap W=V(\mathfrak q)$. This nonempty open subset is dense in $C$, and the point $\mathfrak q$ is generic in $V(\mathfrak q)$, so its closure in $Y$ is $C$. Continuity gives $\overline{\{g(\mathfrak q)\}}=\overline{g(C)}=D$, an irreducible component of $X$ by hypothesis: the equality follows by applying continuity to $C=\overline{\{\mathfrak q\}}$ and using the reverse inclusion from $\mathfrak q\in C$. Since $g(\mathfrak q)\in U$, closure in the open subspace gives $\overline{\{g(\mathfrak q)\}}^{U}=D\cap U$; the open-component lemma makes this an irreducible component of $U$. Under the affine spectrum correspondence its prime is $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$, which is therefore a minimal prime of $A$.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, proof of (4), contraction of minimal primes; elementary topological justification expanded

proof.text: Let $s$ be a nonzerodivisor of $A$. The reduced-ring nonzerodivisor criterion says $s$ lies in no minimal prime of $A$. Step 3 shows $\varphi(s)$ lies in no minimal prime of $B$, so the same criterion for the reduced ring $B$ makes $\varphi(s)$ a nonzerodivisor. There is consequently a ring homomorphism $\Phi:Q(A)\to Q(B)$ given by $a/s\mapsto\varphi(a)/\varphi(s)$. To verify well-definedness directly, an equality of source fractions gives $u(ta-sb)=0$ for a nonzerodivisor $u$; applying $\varphi$ gives exactly the localization equivalence for the image fractions, since $\varphi(u)$ is again a nonzerodivisor. Addition, multiplication and the unit are preserved by the displayed fraction formulas. No injectivity of $\varphi$ or $\Phi$ is asserted or needed.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, proof of (4), canonical total-fraction map; explicit fraction calculation

proof.text:
For $z\in\overline A$, apply $\Phi$ to a monic equation for $z$ over $A$. This is a monic equation for $\Phi(z)$ with coefficients in the image of $B$, so $\Phi(z)$ is integral over $B$. The normal-ring total-fractions lemma now puts $\Phi(z)$ in the image of $B	o Q(B)$. This localization map is injective: if $b/1=0$, a nonzerodivisor annihilates $b$, so $b=0$. Thus $\Phi|_{\overline A}$ has a unique codomain restriction $\psi:\overline A	o B$. It is a ring map because the inclusion $B	o Q(B)$ is injective, and $\psi(a/1)=\varphi(a)$. Applying the contravariant affine spectrum correspondence gives a morphism $h_W:W	o
u^{-1}(U)\subseteq X^
u$ whose composition with $
u$ is $g|_W$.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, proof of (4), integral closure maps into the normal ring; Tag 034M through the cited node

proof.text: Here is the omitted local uniqueness check. Every factorization $W\to X^\nu$ over $g|_W$ has image in the open $\nu^{-1}(U)$ and is therefore an $A$-algebra map $\theta:\overline A\to B$ on rings. For $z\in\overline A\subseteq Q(A)$ choose $z=a/s$ with $s$ a nonzerodivisor of $A$. Since $\overline A$ is a subring of $Q(A)$ containing the image of $A$, $sz=a$ holds in $\overline A$ itself. Applying $\theta$ forces $\varphi(s)\theta(z)=\varphi(a)$. Step 4 says $\varphi(s)$ is a nonzerodivisor in $B$, so this equation has at most one solution for $\theta(z)$. Both $\psi(z)$ and $\theta(z)$ solve it; thus $\theta(z)=\psi(z)$ for every $z$, and the affine spectrum correspondence gives uniqueness of $h_W$.

source.place: Tag 035Q, label lemma-normalization-normal, final sentence of proof (4): omitted uniqueness supplied by cancellation

proof.text:
The maps $h_W$ agree on overlaps. Given a point $y\in W_i\cap W_j$, choose an affine open $U_0\subseteq U_i\cap U_j$ containing $g(y)$ and an affine open $W_0\subseteq W_i\cap W_j\cap g^{-1}(U_0)$ containing $y$. Each restricted lift has image in $
u^{-1}(U_0)$; steps 2--6 were proved for every affine pair with $g(W)\subseteq U$, so their uniqueness calculation applies to $(W_0,U_0)$ and makes the restrictions equal. Equality on this open covering implies equality on the whole overlap by the gluing lemma. The same lemma glues all $h_W$ to $h:Y	o X^
u$, with $
u\circ h=g$ because the equality holds on the cover. Any other lift agrees on every $W$ by step 6, hence equals $h$ globally. This uses arbitrary open coverings, so no quasi-compactness of $Y$ is required. For $Y=\varnothing$ the empty covering in the same gluing lemma gives the unique empty-source morphism.
